articleTitle: “Training in the engineering branch of the post office“
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Mr. President and gentlemen, I should like to thank contributors to the discussion for their kind remarks. I am glad Mr. Machanik used his considerable influence to lay that ghost of spoon-feeding. I have heard the same remark with reference to our present scheme. I also heard it some 20 to 25 years ago, and Mr. Goodacre has given you a hint as to how the scheme of those days worked I Some of the apprentice courses are easy, and some are the reverse. Some become more complicated every day with the development of new devices and the introduction of new methods and new materials. The days when enough knowledge and skill could be picked up as one went along are far behind us. There are several branches of communication engineering each of which is worthy of a lifetime's study. The apprentices are given an introduction, and we try to give them a sound foundation. They are given enough to enable them to perform an electrician's or a mechanician's duties with reasonable competence, but little more. For a really intelligent understanding of what they are doing and why, a great deal of private study is essential, and I am afraid many of them do not realise this. People who think the boys are spoon-fed are really very ignorant of the facts, or simply succumbing to that human failing of envy for the one who has a better opportunity than one had oneself. The fact is that unless these better opportunities are afforded the department will be unable to discharge its responsibilities properly.

articleTitle: South African standards institution
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Some time ago the Radio Manufacturers' Association prepared two specifications for capacitors, one dealing with the rating and dimensions of paper and electrolytic capacitors, and the other with the colour coding of capacitors. These two specifications have now been combined into a single document and published by the British Standards Institution as War Emergency British Standard 271-1941. This is in effect a revision of the specification issued in 1926 for Fixed Capacitors for Radio Reception Purposes, and its object is to provide a limited range of sizes and types of condensers to be manufactured in war-time. It is considered that this restricted range will meet all the normal requirements of the industry under war-time conditions.

articleTitle: An outline of the electrolytic corrosion of buried metallic structures
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: It is not very many years ago that the corrosion of metals was considered, more or less, as an unavoidable evil, but the enormous field for saving directed the attention of the world's scientific workers to this subject, with the resultant development of the electro-chemical theory of corrosion, which is now generally accepted as the one best explaining a multitude of facts concerning the corrosion of metals. This theory suggests that all corrosion is due to the flow of current through an electrolyte connecting the anodic and cathodic areas. It is not the intention of this paper to discuss metallic corrosion in general, but to outline briefly that small, although important section of the problem which affects the life of buried metallic structures, such as cable sheaths, water and gas pipes, concrete reinforcing, etc., and which is commonly known as “Electrolytic Corrosion.”

abstract: This essay describes briefly the growth of the Salisbury, Southern Rhodesia, Municipal Electricity Department. It shows that this growth has followed almost exactly an exponential law. articleTitle: “Factors influencing electric power transmission on the reef”
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Mr. President and gentlemen, all who are interested in the methods employed on the Rand for effectively coping with lightning problems on transmission lines will have read with pleasure the contributions by Dr. Bernard Price and Mr. V. Pickles. These contributors have supplemented the paper and added value to it by summarising and analysing the experience gained and the progress achieved during the past 30 years in combating the effects of lightning. In addition, Dr. Price has explained the results of an experiment which was conducted recently on two adjacent 88 kV transmission lines, the object of which was to obtain a better understanding of the behaviour of overhead guard wires under lightning conditions. The results have thrown new light on this intriguing problem.

publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: It is necessary to consider the factors local to the Salisbury Municipal Undertaking in order to appreciate the reasons for developing a reinforced concrete method of transmission line standard construction. Table No. 1 details meteorological data from which several pertinent facts emerge, The maximum recorded wind velocities show low figures with one gust of short duration up to 80 m.p.h.; steady high winds have so far not been recorded. The average wind direction and the temperature limits are additional factors favouring a reconsideration of the standards adopted by regulation or statute elsewhere. Severe lightning is experienced during the rainy season from November to April.
